newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian rebels see hostage talks progressing.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian rebels see hostage talks progressing.

text.p: The Marxist guerrilla group holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home said on Monday talks to end the siege were progressing because the government realised the only solution was to negotiate.

With talks deadlocked since early March, President Alberto Fujimori was under growing pressure to find a peaceful outcome to the 97-day crisis, Isaac Velazco, the rebels' international spokesman, told Reuters.
"The greatest achievement in the last 15 to 20 days has been the government's recognition that the only solution is through negotiation," Velazco said by telephone from Germany.
"The government does not have much time as it liked to claim earlier. It is now under a lot of pressure from abroad -- particularly from Japan."

President Alberto Fujimori has said throughout the standoff he is patient enough to wait months for a peaceful solution. He issued a statement on Monday saying the end of the crisis was "not in sight," after a meeting at the presidential palace with a mediator, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani.
Cipriani and Fujimori discussed negotiations and "agreed on the need for greater efforts in that area, although the date for the end of it was not in sight," said the statement.
But there were signs Fujimori was willing to make some concessions to speed negotiations.

A Peruvian newspaper reported on Monday the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) may be offered a multi-million dollar ransom, asylum in the Caribbean and the release of some of its jailed comrades in return for freeing the hostages.
The proposal was drawn up by the three-member negotiating commission and would be presented to the government and the rebels "in coming days," the daily La Republica said.
MRTA spokesman Velazco said the offer was "feasible, could be studied and lead to a solution to the crisis as long as it considers the freedom of our jailed fighters and leaders."
Rebel leader Nestor Cerpa made a formal proposal to the government detailing which prisoners the group wanted freed, Velazco said without elaboration.

Since the rebels stormed the diplomatic residence and seized hundreds of hostages on Dec. 17, 1996, they have publicly insisted on the release of up to 450 jailed comrades. But MRTA members have also said a reduced number of releases could be negotiated as long as those freed were high-ranking comrades.
Visits by negotiators to jailed MRTA members raised speculation the government was compiling a list of rebels it might be prepared to release.

Tokyo suggested this sort of behind-the-scenes work was bringing the crisis closer to a solution, despite only one face-to-face meeting between the hostage-takers and the government in more than two weeks.

"The situation may appear deadlocked at first sight, but I am convinced that the issue is heading towards a solution," Japanese Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura told reporters in Tokyo on Monday. "I think the time is ripe for a peaceful settlement."
Komura was just back from a trip to discuss the crisis with Fujimori and secure formal agreements from Cuba and the Dominican Republic to give the hostage-takers asylum if the MRTA agreed.
The guerrillas reserved comment but Velazco said it would be acceptable if part of a deal to free prisoners.

"If the unit (at the residence) and our prisoners have to leave the country for there to be a solution to the crisis, we have no problem with that," he said. "We will know when the time is right to return."
Among the captives aere Fujimori's younger brother, two government ministers, and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
